summary:
Price tracking stops being something you switch on. Any wishlisted item with a product link is checked daily, and the first successful check turns tracking on by itself (`apply_price_observation`). Owners can still switch it off, which is now recorded explicitly in a new column, `price_tracking_disabled_by_user`, so the scheduler can tell *you said no* apart from *not working yet* and *auto-paused*.

The scheduler also changes shape: due items are grouped by store, each store's items still run one at a time with the jittered delay, and up to 8 stores run at once (`check_tracked_prices` → `_check_domain_group`). Repeated failures now pause an item after 3 attempts instead of 5, whether or not it ever had a price.

The risk is in the migration: everyone who turned tracking off before this change is about to be opted back in.

steps.title: Tracking turns on when a check succeeds
steps.body: This is the whole idea in five lines. A price we could read proves the page is trackable, so a successful check enables tracking and clears any pause, unless the owner opted out.

steps.title: The owner's no is now a fact in the database
steps.body: Before this change "off" could mean three things. `price_tracking_disabled_by_user` names the one that must stick. The migration adds it with a default of false, which is where finding #1 lives.

steps.title: The scheduler skips opt-outs and paused items
steps.body: Every item gets its own session, and an opt-out or a pause short-circuits before any request is made.

steps.title: Grouped by store, stores in parallel
steps.body: Due items are bucketed by `_domain_key`, then `asyncio.gather` runs one `_check_domain_group` per store, at most 8 at a time. The fetch is async (`await fetch_current_price`), so the concurrency is real.

steps.title: Inside a store, nothing changed
steps.body: Same serial loop and jittered delay as the old job, so any one site sees the same request pattern as before. That promise depends on `_domain_key` putting one site in one bucket (finding #2).

steps.title: Failing pages stop being retried
steps.body: Three consecutive failures pause the item and notify the owner, for items that never had a price too. Without this, automatic tracking would retry an unreadable page forever.

notes.title: Everyone who turned tracking off is opted back in
notes.body: The new column defaults to `false` for every existing row. An item whose owner switched tracking off before this change has `price_tracking_enabled = false` and no pause, which now reads as *not established yet*. The next daily check succeeds, `apply_price_observation` turns tracking back on, and price-change notifications resume for something the owner explicitly silenced.
notes.fix: Backfill in `upgrade()`: items that had a verified price and are off without a pause were turned off by their owner.
notes.impact: Owners who opted out start getting price notifications again the day this deploys, with no way to tell why.

suggestion.code:
op.add_column(
        'wishlistitem',
        sa.Column(
            'price_tracking_disabled_by_user',
            sa.Boolean(),
            server_default='false',
            nullable=False,
        ),
    )
    # Off, not paused, and once verified: the owner turned it off.
    op.execute(
        "UPDATE wishlistitem SET price_tracking_disabled_by_user = true "
        "WHERE price_tracking_enabled = false AND price_tracking_paused_at IS NULL "
        "AND price_verified_at IS NOT NULL"
    )

notes.title: www.amazon.com and amazon.com count as two stores
notes.body: `urlparse(...).netloc.lower()` keeps `www.` and ports. Links pasted from different places for one store (`https://www.amazon.com/...` and `https://amazon.com/...`) land in two groups, so that store is hit concurrently, which is exactly what the grouping promises not to do.
notes.fix: Normalize the host: `urlparse(product_url).hostname or ""`, then strip a leading `www.`.
notes.impact: Bursts against the biggest store, the one most likely to rate-limit or block.

notes.title: Group by store instead of a global rate limiter
notes.body: Per-store groups keep each site's request pattern identical to the old serial job while total time shrinks with the number of stores.

alternatives.option: One global queue with a smaller delay
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but every site sees faster requests, which is the scrape burst the delay exists to avoid.

alternatives.option: A per-host token bucket shared across workers
alternatives.tradeoff: Right at scale; heavy for one scheduler process checking a few hundred items a day.

notes.title: Why 3 failures and not 5
notes.body: With tracking automatic, every link is a candidate, including pages that never had a readable price. Five tries meant five days of pointless requests per unreadable link; three still rides out a one-off outage.

notes.title: Is one scheduler process the expected deployment?
notes.body: The concurrency cap and per-store serialization are per process. If the worker ever runs as more than one replica, each replica builds its own groups and the same store gets hit in parallel. I assumed one worker; is that right?

outgoingBody:
Nice change: automatic tracking with an explicit opt-out is the right model, and the per-store grouping keeps each site's request pattern exactly as it was.

One thing must change before this deploys: the migration opts everyone who turned tracking off back in. The store-key comment is a one-line normalization so one store can't land in two groups.
